\chapter{Travelling --- Asking, Boarding, Staying, and When It Goes Wrong}
\label{ch:viajar}
\hlchaptermodality{268}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask where something is, ask for a ticket and a room, and say that there is a problem.}

Complete ES-C268-problema: put each of the chapter's three nouns into the donde esta frame, ask for a ticket and a room outright, and report a problem with the correct article.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[¿dónde está?]{¿dónde está? — the question that unsticks you}

\label{lesson:ES-C268-donde-esta}



\begin{quote}
You know \emph{dónde}, and you know \emph{está}. Put them together and you have the single most useful sentence a traveller owns — the one that works when you are lost, when you cannot find the door, when the platform is not where the sign said it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item dónde — the asking word, with its written accent.
  \item estar — the \emph{being} that is about \textbf{place}, not essence.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Two stressed syllables: \emph{DÓN-de es-TÁ}. Both accents are written, and both are telling you the truth about your voice. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{¿dónde está?} — \textquotedblleft{}where is it?\textquotedblright{} Two known words, no new grammar:

\emph{dónde} (\textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{está} (\textquotedblleft{}it is, located\textquotedblright{}). Spanish has two verbs for \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and this question takes \emph{estar}, the one that answers \emph{where} rather than \emph{what}. A thing's location can change; \emph{estar} is the verb for what changes.

Say the name of what you want after it and the question is finished: \emph{¿dónde está el hotel?}, \emph{¿dónde está el tren?} You do not need to build a sentence — you need one frame and a noun.

\textbf{Where it comes from.} \emph{Dónde} is Latin \emph{unde}, \textquotedblleft{}from where,\textquotedblright{} with a \emph{de-} welded on the front; \emph{está} is Latin \emph{stare}, \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{} — the same root inside English \textbf{stand}, \textbf{state} and \textbf{stay}. Spanish asks, quite literally, \emph{where does it stand?}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is a \textbf{frame}: a fixed opening you finish with whatever you need. The next three lessons give you three nouns worth putting in it.

Two courtesies make it land better, and you already have both. Open with \emph{perdón} and the stranger knows a question is coming. Close with \emph{gracias} whether or not you understood the answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿dónde está?} — stress DÓN and TÁ
  \item the same question about the hotel — \emph{¿dónde está el hotel?}
  \item it again, opening with \emph{perdón}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} verbs does this question use, and why? (\emph{Estar} — it is about place, and place changes.) What Latin verb is \emph{está}? (\emph{Stare}, \textquotedblleft{}to stand.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[billete]{billete — the ticket, and the note in your pocket}

\label{lesson:ES-C268-billete}



\begin{quote}
One word gets you onto the train. It also, confusingly and usefully, means the paper money you pay for it with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ¿dónde está? — the frame this noun drops into.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Three syllables, stress in the middle: \emph{bi-YE-te}. The \emph{ll} is a \emph{y} sound in most of the Spanish-speaking world. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{billete} — \textquotedblleft{}ticket,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}banknote.\textquotedblright{} One word, two things you carry, and the overlap is not an accident: both are a small official paper that entitles you to something.

\textbf{Where it comes from.} Latin \emph{bulla} was a \textbf{seal} — the blob of wax stamped onto a document to prove it was genuine. The sealed document took the seal's name, shrank through French \emph{billet} (\textquotedblleft{}a short note\textquotedblright{}), and arrived in Spanish as \emph{billete}. The same \emph{bulla} is still sitting inside English \textbf{bulletin} and the papal \textbf{bull}: all of them are documents that were once literally sealed.

\textbf{Worth knowing before you travel.} Much of Latin America says \textbf{boleto} or \textbf{pasaje} for a travel ticket and keeps \emph{billete} for money. Both are correct Spanish; which one you hear depends on where you are standing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Drop it into the frame — \emph{¿dónde está el billete?} — or ask for one outright: \emph{un billete, por favor}. Two words and a courtesy is a complete transaction.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{billete} — stress the middle, \emph{bi-YE-te}
  \item ask for one — \emph{un billete, por favor}
  \item the Latin American word for a travel ticket (\emph{boleto})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{bulla} mean? (A seal.) What two things does \emph{billete} name? (A ticket, and a banknote.) Which English words still carry \emph{bulla}? (\textbf{Bulletin}, and a papal \textbf{bull}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[habitación]{habitación — a room, from a verb meaning to live somewhere}

\label{lesson:ES-C268-habitacion}



\begin{quote}
The word you need at a hotel desk. It is long, but it is built out of a verb you can almost read already.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item billete — the previous thing you had to ask for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Five syllables, stress at the very end: \emph{a-bi-ta-SYON}. The written accent on \emph{ó} is the whole reason you know that. The \emph{h} is silent — it always is. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{habitación} — \textquotedblleft{}room.\textquotedblright{} Take it apart and the meaning is transparent:

\emph{habitar} (\textquotedblleft{}to live in, to dwell\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-ción} (the ending that turns a verb into the noun for its result). So a \emph{habitación} is, literally, \textbf{a place lived in}.

That \emph{-ción} is one of the most profitable endings in the language, and it is English \emph{-tion} wearing different clothes: \emph{nación} / nation, \emph{estación} / station, \emph{información} / information. Meet it once and hundreds of words open up.

\textbf{Where it comes from.} Latin \emph{habitare}, \textquotedblleft{}to dwell\textquotedblright{} — a frequentative of \emph{habere}, \textquotedblleft{}to have,\textquotedblright{} so it once meant something like \textquotedblleft{}to keep on having a place.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{inhabit} and \textbf{habitat} are the same root, undisguised.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Una habitación, por favor} books you a room. And the \emph{-ción} ending you just met is a key you will use far outside this chapter: these nouns are feminine, and they are very often an English \emph{-tion} word you already know with its ending swapped.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{habitación} — silent \emph{h}, stress the last syllable
  \item ask for a room — \emph{una habitación, por favor}
  \item two more \emph{-ción} words and their English twins
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the verb \emph{habitar} mean? (To dwell, to live in.) What does \emph{-ción} do? (Turns a verb into the noun for its result.) Which article do \emph{-ción} nouns take? (\emph{La} — they are feminine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — three phrases, in the order you need them}

\label{lesson:ES-C268-repaso-llegar-y-quedarse}



\begin{quote}
The first thing you say anywhere new. (\emph{¿Dónde está?})
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
These three arrived one after another, and they are not a list. They are a sequence.

\textbf{¿Dónde está?} — you find the thing. \textbf{Un billete} — you buy your way onto it. \textbf{Una habitación} — you stop, and sleep.

Find, travel, rest. Said in any other order they still work, but said in that order they are a day.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\emph{Habitación} is the long one, and it is the one that pays you back.

Take it apart: \emph{habitar}, \textquotedblleft{}to live in,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{-ción}, the ending that turns a doing word into the noun for its result. A \emph{habitación} is, with no metaphor at all, \textbf{a place lived in}.

That ending is the profitable part. It does the same job every time it appears, it makes the noun feminine every time, and it is very often an English word you already own wearing different clothes — the English ending is \emph{-tion}.

And \emph{habitar} has a story of its own. It is Latin \emph{habitāre}, built off \emph{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to have,\textquotedblright{} in a form that means doing something over and over. To dwell somewhere is to \textbf{keep on having} a place. English \textbf{inhabit} and \textbf{habitat} are the same root, barely disguised.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{¿dónde está?} · \emph{un billete} · \emph{una habitación}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{habitación}, taken literally? (\textbf{A place lived in}.) What did \emph{habitar} grow out of? (\emph{\textbf{Habēre}}, to have.) And what do you ask for before you ever need the room? (\textbf{Un \emph{billete}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[problema]{problema — the word for when it goes wrong (and the -a that is masculine)}

\label{lesson:ES-C268-problema}



\begin{quote}
Travel goes wrong. This is the word that starts the conversation about it — and it hides a grammatical surprise you should meet on purpose rather than by accident.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item habitación — and the gender rule it followed.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Four syllables, stress in the middle: \emph{pro-BLE-ma}. No written accent, because that is where a word ending in a vowel is stressed by default. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{problema} — \textquotedblleft{}problem.\textquotedblright{} A near-twin of the English word, and you will be understood the moment you say it.

\textbf{Where it comes from.} Greek \emph{próblēma}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing thrown forward\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pro-} (\textquotedblleft{}forward\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{bállein} (\textquotedblleft{}to throw\textquotedblright{}). A problem is something pitched into your path. That same \emph{bállein} is inside English \textbf{ballistic} and \textbf{symbol}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Here is the surprise, and it is worth more than the word itself. You learned that nouns ending in \emph{-a} are usually feminine. \emph{Problema} is \textbf{masculine}: \emph{el problema}, \emph{un problema}. Never \emph{la problema}.

It is not an exception you have to memorise blindly — it is a whole family with a shared history. Greek nouns ending in \emph{-ma} were neuter, and when Latin borrowed them the neuter words landed on the masculine side. Every one of them came into Spanish the same way: \emph{el problema}, \emph{el sistema}, \emph{el tema}, \emph{el programa}, \emph{el idioma}, \emph{el clima}. If a noun ends in \emph{-ma} and sounds Greek and academic, guess \emph{el} and you will usually be right.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un problema} — and notice you did not say \emph{una}
  \item report one — \emph{perdón, hay un problema}
  \item three more \emph{-ma} words that take \emph{el}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which article does \emph{problema} take, and why? (\emph{El} — Greek \emph{-ma} nouns were neuter and became masculine.) What did \emph{próblēma} mean literally? (A thing thrown forward.) Name two more of the family. (\emph{El sistema}, \emph{el tema}, \emph{el programa}, \emph{el idioma}, \emph{el clima}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — when the ending tells the truth, and when it lies}

\label{lesson:ES-C268-repaso-dos-finales-dos-generos}



\begin{quote}
\emph{La habitación.} \emph{El problema.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two words from the same chapter, and they disagree about the most basic question you can ask a Spanish noun.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{article} \\
\midrule
\emph{habitación} & \emph{-ción} & \textbf{la} \\
\emph{problema} & \emph{-ma} & \textbf{el} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One of those two endings predicts the article. The other does the opposite of what you were taught to expect.

\emph{-ción} is one of the most reliable signals in the language: it is feminine, every time, without exception you will meet. And \emph{-a}, the ending you were taught to read as feminine, hands you \emph{el problema}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The useful part is that neither of these is arbitrary, so neither has to be memorised as a bare fact.

\emph{-ción} is feminine because the Latin ending it descends from was feminine, and nothing since has disturbed it. The ending kept its gender the whole way down.

\emph{Problema} is masculine because it did not come through Latin from the start. It came from \textbf{Greek}, where nouns ending in \emph{-ma} were neither masculine nor feminine but a third thing — neuter. Latin had no comfortable place to put them and handed them to the masculine, and Spanish inherited that decision.

So \emph{-ma} is not an exception to the \emph{-a} rule. It is a \textbf{passport stamp}: it tells you the word came in from Greek, and the gender came with it. When you meet another noun in \emph{-ma} that names an idea, expect \emph{el}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la habitación} · \emph{el problema}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending always tells you \emph{la}? (\emph{\textbf{-ción}}.) Why is \emph{problema} masculine? (\textbf{It is Greek — \emph{-ma} nouns were neuter, and Latin made them masculine}.) Is that an exception or a family? (\textbf{A family}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
